speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in December last the Government invoked the meat import law and limited beef imports this year to 146.5 million pounds. This was in response to the EEC countries shipping 51 million pounds of beef into Canada subsidized by up to 48 cents a pound. When the United States complained about its quota of 21 million pounds, the Government capitulated and has agreed to increase that to 65 million pounds. It got nothing in return, selling out the farmers in Canada. Now the EEC is demanding that its quota be raised to 33 million pounds or the EEC will impose a countervailing duty of $50 million on farm commodities being sold to Europe.
When the Government capitulates to the EEC, the new quotas for beef will rise to 216 million pounds, the largest ever, and we will have seen the most cowardly retreat by the Government of Canada in history. It is time the Government of Canada summoned its courage, marched into the GATT tribunal in Geneva, and started fighting for Canadian farmers.

Mr. Speaker, over the years Canadians have, from time to time, complained about harassment of their visitors arriving at Pearson International Airport. During the past year these complaints have increased. They have been regularly denied by the administration, even in answer to MP's letters.
Now officers are complaining that they are being harassed, that their performance is being measured by the number of visitors they send for inquiry or send to detention under bond.
Two months ago a complaint was sent to the Minister. Six weeks ago an internal report was made to the Minister. No action was taken until after a Globe and Mail story. The Minister has now promised an independent inquiry. I call upon
the Minister to make sure that it is genuinely independent, that it has an impartial chairperson, and a representative of the union, the CEIV, who represents the employees at the airport, and that witnesses, especially officers of immigration, are invited to testify under oath and under protection of the Canada Evidence Act, and without fear of reprisals. The scope of the inquiry should include all the allegations made by those officers about the treatment to which they are being subjected by their supervisors, and the inquiry should reach up to whatever level is necessary to determine who was responsible for the policy of telling long-term employees that they may not be promoted-
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

subsubtopic: ADMISSION TO CANADA AFTER WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, history is the measure of a civilization. Our history is the criterion which the nations and peoples of the world use to formulate their opinions and pass judgment on the character and social fabric of Canada. I have become disheartened and disillusioned as the media make daily revelations that Canada gave refuge to Nazi war criminals after the war.
The Toronto Star has uncovered evidence in the archives that former Liberal Prime Minister Mackenzie King's Cabinet approved a special order in 1948 allowing war criminals to remain in Canada despite earlier deportation orders. This revelation tends to confirm past suspicions that previous Liberal Governments provided sanctuary for Nazi war criminals and collaborators after World War II. What tragedy and hypocrisy when, during the same period, Jewish survivors of Nazi concentration camps were denied entry!
I urge the Government, for humanity, for the western world, to face up to the challenge, deal with it, and remove this dark cloud over Canada. We must bring these criminals to justice in Canada or overseas so that our brave men did not die in vain. I am certain that the Deschenes Commission will rectify this injustice.

March 22, 1985

subtopic: S O. 21 PENSIONS RETIRED PUBLIC EMPLOYEES-RESTORATION OF PENSION INDEXING BASE ADVOCATED
S O. 21 PENSIONS RETIRED PUBLIC EMPLOYEES-RESTORATION OF PENSION INDEXING BASE ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two years ago the previous Government unilaterally cut the indexing of retired public employees' pensions as part of the six and five restraint program. My Party fought that measure in committee and in this House, and considered it a flagrant disregard for an agreement between employer and employees. Thankfully this program of cut-backs and austerity has ended, but the damage done to retired federal employees' pensions will remain in perpetuity.
The base rate of a federal retired employee's pension has been permanently reduced by the difference between six and five and the inflation rate at that time. As a result, some
200,000	former federal employees are losing substantial portions of their pension benefits. While Canadians are glad to see that the rate of inflation has fallen, Mr. Speaker, indications are that this has occurred due to long-term economic trends and external factors, such as international interest rates. I therefore strongly urge the Government to look at the viability of restoring the indexing base of pensions for retired federal employees.
I also welcome the willingness of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) to review the pension system. In addition, on behalf of Canada's excellent and dedicated Public Service, I sincerely hope that no Government will again introduce such a regressive measure.

Mr. Speaker, the main concern of Canadians is still unemployment and jobs. Last November's economic statement and other government initiatives such as Investment Canada have begun to create a new climate for medium and long-term growth. However, Canadians want short-term solutions as well.
The up-coming Budget cannot deal with unemployment in isolation. It must also take into account our unprecedented peacetime deficit and national debt, abnormally high interest rates, the value of the Canadian dollar, and the possibility of renewed inflationary pressure.
In order to solve these problems we must have a plan of action upon which most Canadians can agree. This is why the National Economic Conference, now taking place here in Ottawa, is so important for all of us. It provides a forum for business, labour, consumers, native people, church leaders, ethnic groups, social service agencies, the unemployed, and voluntary organizations, to discuss their solutions not just with the Government but with each other. Hopefully a consensus will emerge and the up-coming Budget will provide a formula which will get Canada moving again.

subsubtopic: PINE TREE LINE-ANNOUNCED CLOSURE OF DANA, SASK., STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever since Canadian Forces Station Dana, Saskatchewan, was established in 1962, it has played a very important role in the local economy of the village of Dana and the surrounding district. I have been notified by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) that on March 13, 1985, the Conservative Government decided to close the stations which comprise the Pine Tree network. The actual date for Dana will be announced within the next three years.
This closure represents a very serious setback to Dana and area. The jobs of the 120 military personnel are not threat-
March 22, 1985

ened; of course they will be reassigned within the Department of National Defence. However, approximately 65 direct jobs and five indirect civilian jobs are affected, and it will be extremely difficult for those 70 individuals to find new work and for the area to maintain its level of services to people, with such a large loss in revenue. Also, a centre for community activity will no longer be available and the village of Dana and surrounding area will suffer greatly. No job offers have been made to the civilian staff. A six-month notice is all that will be offered prior to the actual closure.
I appeal to the Government, on behalf of all those individuals and families who will be hurt as a result of this closure, to provide real assistance in locating alternate employment. I urge the Government to take a hard look at the economic and social costs of these closures across the country, and to provide real economic assistance, instead of merely stating its intention to close down the stations.

Mr. Speaker, the Government is living up to its main commitment to listen to Canadians before acting. Since September 4 we have been charting a new course for Canada, characterized by consultation and co-operation. This new direction points to economic renewal and national reconciliation.
In less than seven months consultation papers have been prepared by Ministers seeking public input on a number of significant issues. Our Government has held important summit meetings with the provincial First Ministers, and with the President of the United States, our greatest friend and ally.
Today the process continues with the National Economic Conference. The Government has brought together, for the first time in Canadian history, 136 participants from all walks of life and from all parts of Canada. The voices which will be heard include those of business, labour, consumers, women, native people, church leaders, ethnic groups, social agencies, and the unemployed.
If economic renewal and social justice are to be achieved, it is essential that we work together rather than against each other. That is what the National Economic Conference is all about. It is an integral part of the Government's commitment to change the way decisions are made in our country.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN UNITED STATES SDI RESEARCH PROGRAM
speechtext:

March 22, 1985

subsubtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN UNITED STATES SDI RESEARCH PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as usual the Hon. Member's recollection of what was said, both here and in committee, is quite inaccurate. In the House of Commons, and I believe in committee, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has left doors open. subsubtopic: INCLUSION OF SEVERANCE PAY IN INCOME CALCULATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, take the question as notice, and advise my colleague accordingly so as to provide the Hon. Member with a reply as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out, this measure is to come into force very soon. Many laid-off workers were going to use this severance pay to re-establish themselves in employment, to relocate to other parts of the country, and even to roll it over with an RRSP into their pension provisions. They will now be forced to spend the severance pay on the basic necessities of life rather than using their unemployment insurance.
Does the Minister not agree that this is a very harsh measure which has implications not foreseen? I would ask her and any of the Ministers, including the Deputy Prime Minister, to consult quickly on this so that it can be postponed and so as to enable full consultation to take place before it moves ahead.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Yesterday South African police in an armoured truck, using semi-automatic rifles, shotguns, and machine guns, killed at least 18, and perhaps as many as 43, blacks who were demonstrating in commemoration of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Sharpeville massacre. Some 200 blacks have been killed since last August as the white minority Government attempts to suppress all dissent. Will the Canadian Government now get off the fence and lead an international movement for disinvestment in South Africa?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, that tragic incident of yesterday has demonstrated one more time that the injustice and violence of the apartheid system can only engender further violence. The Government of Canada, and I am sure the people of Canada, deplore this act. We believe the only long-term solution is to move to a non-discriminatory society in South Africa. We are now in the process of reviewing fully the appropriateness of Canadian policy with regard to South Africa. Events of the tragic kind of yesterday add impetus to that review.
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. It is not enough simply to deplore and wait for some kind of long-term solution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will invade them, will we?

Does the Minister not recognize that the actions of the South African Government must make it a pariah, an outcast among all decent nations in the world? What concrete steps is the Government of Canada prepared to take to put pressure on the Government of South Africa to end this tragic situation, instead of just waiting for a long-term solution?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada, under the leadership of different Parties, has given leadership to the world on this question, going back as far as the action of the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker with regard to the expulsion of South Africa from the Commonwealth. We are very conscious, not only of that tradition of governments, but of that concern on the part of Canadians.
We also think it is essential that the actions which Canada might take, or might be involved in, are actions which in fact improve the quality and prospect of life of the majority in South Africa. I have said that we are undertaking a review. We intend to complete that review as quickly as possible. We intend to take action which is consistent with the tradition of
Oral Questions
leadership of Canada with regard to South Africa, and in opposition to the apartheid regime.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. I understand that the Minister has received the Fraser Royal Commission Report on Pornography. Could he advise the House when he will be tabling that report in the House and when he will be introducing legislation to restrict pornography in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad that there are some Members opposite who wish information rather than just making cheap gibes and silly attacks.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The answer is that we have not actually received the Fraser report yet. It is in the Department in bits and pieces getting translated. One consecutive volume has not yet been presented to me so I have not received it yet. I think it should be received by the first week of April. Hopefully we should be able to make it public early in April. We will then have to undertake the matter of reviewing the law in the light of the recommendations and in the light of the Badgley report.
How long?
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentlemen opposite are not interested in the reform of the law in this area, apparently.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. It concerns the statements in an interview with the press some weeks ago on acid rain, and the evolution of arrangements with the provinces. There were some surprised statements, notably on the part of the Minister of Environment for Ontario, in reaction to the fact that for the first time the provinces seem to be expected to participate financially in the modernization of the non ferrous metal industry. Would the Minister inform the House whether the provincial Ministers of the Environment were consulted and informed about her intention to have them participate financially in the modernization of the industry?

March 22, 1985
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Suzanne Blais-Grenier (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, not only were my provincial counterparts informed, they were consulted beforehand, and they were a party to the decision at our meeting on February 5 in Montreal. If the press misreported certain comments, as I think they did, I am afraid I cannot help that, and neither can my provincial counterpart in Ontario.

How does the Minister explain the statement of surprise expressed by the Minister of the Environment for Ontario at the requested participation by him in the modernization of the non ferrous metals industry, as reported in the press?

speakeroldname: Hon. Suzanne Blais-Grenier (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would rather not depend on media reports to find out what my hon. colleague, the Minister of the Environment of Ontario is thinking. All I can say is that yesterday, I received a letter in which he congratulated me on the agreement concluded with the United States in Quebec City.

Mr. Speaker, I have yet another question for the fiscal butcher of the Conservative Party. The Deputy Prime Minister admitted yesterday that he has led a committee of packers and choppers on a search and destroy mission-
Order. I will ask the Member not to repeat that phrase and simply to put his question.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister why the Government chopped $2 million for the creation of the Northern Fishery Development Corporation in Newfoundland? Does the Minister understand that it was in fact an agreement between Canada and Newfoundland? Does he understand that it will help thousands of fishermen in Labrador and Newfoundland? Does he understand that?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman's question is completely wrongly conceived. The question of what will be done to assist the fishermen of northern Newfoundland and Labrador is currently under review by the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, and a decision will be made on that shortly.
Meetings are being held in Newfoundland on that issue. The matter is well in hand, so the Member need have no fear. Furthermore, of course, his own district is about 3,000 miles away from the area so that one wonders why he has this sudden interest in this problem.
Are you not concerned about B.C.?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Where was he when the fishermen of that area were suffering over the last 10 or 12 years, when the election wasn't on?
There is certainly no justice in that statement.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. In fact the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans announced that the Department cut $2 million, and that the funding was not there.
Would the Deputy Prime Minister give us the assurance that the $2 million will be put back on the table, that the commitment to the fishermen of Newfoundland and Labrador will be honoured and the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation will be set up?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am the Acting Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. The Hon. Member may as well learn that now. When the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is not here, I am the Acting Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not used to this adulation, Mr. Speaker.
The answer to the question is that $2 million is not enough. We are not going to restrict the fishermen of northern Newfoundland and Labrador with the meazly $2 million that the hon. gentleman suggests. Much more than that will be necessary to implement these recommendations. Negotiations must first be concluded with the Government of Newfoundland.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to direct my question to the Minister of State (Mines), but first I want to tell the House that, regretfully, we have learned today that the Government is apparently about to give in under pressure by some senior officials and some Members from the Ottawa area, and to reconsider the proposed construction of the cartographic institute in Sherbrooke. All Eastern Townships residents are deeply concerned, wondering what will happen to this project, all the more so since

March 22, 1985

the Prime Minister did make a solemn promise during the election campaign to the effect that the project would be carried out.
Can the Minister allay the fears of Eastern Townships residents and tell us whether construction will go ahead? Yes or no?

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF CARTOGRAPHIC INSTITUTE AT SHERBROOKE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the project to develop the cartographic institute in Sherbrooke, there is presently a training program for the new employees who will be required by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
This project, as is the case with many initiatives of the Government, has been reserved for a financial decision as a result of the task force whose report will be deposited shortly.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be hard pressed to say that the answer is crystal clear. Perhaps I should attempt to elicit a clearer response from the President of the Treasury Board.
What with inaction in the Domtar file, and now in the matter of the cartographic institute, everybody in the Eastern Townships is worried. Would the Minister enlighten us about the economic development policy of the Government of Canada-if there is one-with respect to the Province of Quebec? Is the Government taking concerted action to promote economic development in Quebec?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to answer yes to the question, our Government is taking concerted action to promote economic development in Quebec. Indeed it might very well explain why unemployment in Quebec declined by 54,000 in the past year, more than in any other Canadian province.

Mr. Speaker, as part of the already more than $5 billion CF-18 interceptor purchase, McDonnell Douglas was to undertake a tourism promotion campaign for Canada. Can the Minister of Tourism inform the House what specific initiatives McDonnell Douglas has taken?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. To my knowledge, the company has not approached me directly, nor has it approached my Ministry. I will look into the subject for him and would be prepared to discuss it when the information is gathered.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure that the Minister will indeed undertake that step to which he has just committed himself. I look forward to learn what he discovers.
Perhaps he can assure us that McDonnell Douglas' advertising is of higher quality than the recent advertisements of his Department, which are not promoting tourism in Canada but simply the Minister's handsome, smiling face, and a rather insubstantial consultation paper.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his compliment. The fact is that tourism is an $18 billion a year business. Under the previous Government Canada lost one-half of the country's share of world business receipts.
We believe that we can turn that situation around but we do not believe that the Government has all the answers. Some of the answers reside in the tourism industry itself. That is why we are consulting with the industry, to seek their views through the consultative process, and that is why we published the advertisement in connection with it.
